images.title: Angles that fill 360°
images.purpose: Recap the test for a regular polygon tiling the plane: copies of its angle must add to exactly 360° at a corner.
images.composition: A neat three row table centred in the frame, each row starting with a small flat polygon icon, with generous white space round the table.
exact_structure: A table with exactly 3 rows and 3 columns, thin grey (#6B7280) lines, no header row.
Row 1: a small teal (#0072B2) square icon, then 90°, then × 4 = 360°.
Row 2: a small amber (#E69F00) equilateral triangle icon, then 60°, then × 6 = 360°.
Row 3: a small green (#009E73) regular hexagon icon, then 120°, then × 3 = 360°.
The three 360° values written in reddish purple (#CC79A7).
rejection: a pairing other than square with 90° and × 4, triangle with 60° and × 6, hexagon with 120° and × 3
more or fewer than 3 rows, or any other polygon shown
the hexagon icon drawn with other than 6 sides
images.takeaway: Squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons tile the plane because 90°, 60° and 120° each go into 360° exactly.
images.description: A three row table: a square with 90° × 4 = 360°, a triangle with 60° × 6 = 360°, and a hexagon with 120° × 3 = 360°.
images.context: Shown beside the practice concept on which shapes tile the plane.
images.teaching_notes: Ask students to multiply each angle by the number of copies and check that every row reaches 360°.

image_decisions.why: A small table recaps why only three regular polygons fill 360° at a corner.
